vignette:
He is 22, a quiet young man who works long hours as a junior auditor, the kind of person who finds comfort in order. He talks about spreadsheets the way some people talk about music: cells balanced, figures tied out, small discrepancies tracked down and explained. Before the assault, he likes the predictability of his work. He is single, lives with two male cousins in a small apartment, sends money home when he can, and keeps most things about himself private. He says that privacy has always felt safer.

The rape happens after a work gathering during his first busy season. His team goes out for drinks after finishing a demanding client deadline. He does not usually stay late, but that night he wants to seem easygoing, part of the group. One of the older men from a related department offers him a ride when the evening ends. He remembers feeling relieved not to deal with the train so late. In the car, conversation turns personal in a way that makes him uneasy. He tells himself he is overreacting, that he should not offend someone more senior. When the man pulls over instead of driving him home, he freezes. Later, when he tries to describe it, he does not begin with fear but with confusion: the disbelief that his own body stops responding, that his voice seems to disappear, that his mind narrows to tiny details-the smell of the upholstery, the pressure in his chest, the sound of his own breathing. Afterward, the man tells him not to make trouble, reminds him how things can be misunderstood. He gets out of the car feeling split off from himself, as if he is watching someone else walk to the apartment.

In the days after, he goes to work as if nothing has happened. He showers repeatedly. He throws away the clothes he wore that night and then feels panicked that getting rid of them means he has done something wrong. He barely sleeps. When he closes his eyes, he is back in the car, not always seeing the whole scene but reliving pieces of it with brutal clarity. He starts arriving early to the office so he can avoid elevators crowded with men. If he hears that particular colleague's name, his stomach drops. During audits, he used to pride himself on concentration, but now he loses his place in invoices and rereads the same line over and over. A manager notices unusual errors in his workpapers, and he feels a hot wave of shame that seems bigger than the mistake itself.

He tells no one. Part of his silence comes from humiliation; part of it comes from the world he imagines around him. He expects disbelief, or pity, or some terrible curiosity. He worries what it would mean as a man, as someone raised to be strong and careful with his reputation, to say aloud that another man raped him. He begins to avoid friends from work and family calls from home. When his mother asks why he sounds tired, he says busy season is intense. This is true, but not in the way she means.

Over the next several months, his life contracts. He changes his route to work and scans parking lots without realizing he is doing it. If a client meeting is moved unexpectedly, his chest tightens and he becomes irritable for the rest of the day. He stops going to the gym because the locker room leaves him feeling exposed and suddenly furious. He drinks alone some nights to force himself to sleep, then wakes before dawn, heart racing, convinced for a few seconds that he is back there. He startles when his cousins enter a room without knocking. He keeps his bedroom door locked, then lies awake listening for footsteps.

What troubles him nearly as much as the memories is the way he has begun to think about himself. He calls himself weak for freezing. He replays small decisions from that night-the extra drink, accepting the ride, not leaving sooner-as if enough review could produce a cleaner version of events. As an auditor, he is trained to look for where control failed, where a process broke down. His mind turns that habit against him. He searches for the error and always finds himself.

By the time he comes in, nearly a year has passed. He still performs well enough at work that others describe him as dependable, but he is exhausted by the effort it takes to appear unchanged. He sits stiffly at first, eyes fixed on the floor, speaking in clipped facts. Gradually a fuller story emerges. He describes how certain colognes make his throat close, how being touched unexpectedly can fill him with panic before thought arrives, how he sometimes goes numb during ordinary conversations and realizes he has missed entire minutes. He says the worst part is not only remembering, but never knowing when his body will remember for him. Even now, in a profession built on evidence and explanation, he lives with something that still feels both undeniable and impossible.
